prompt: Put each name on the shape it belongs to.
hint: The one with a dashed line is where trust changes.

prompt: In a data flow diagram, what does a circle stand for?

choices.text: A person outside the system
choices.why: That is an external entity, a rectangle.

choices.text: A process: code that acts on data
choices.why: Right: code that does something with data.

choices.text: A database or a bucket
choices.why: Data at rest is two parallel lines.

choices.text: A place where trust changes
choices.why: That is the dashed boundary line.

prompt: A flow in somebody's diagram is labelled HTTPS. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the protocol is encrypted
choices.why: Encryption says nothing about what is carried, and threats depend on that.

choices.text: Protocols are drawn as boundaries in a data flow diagram
choices.why: Boundaries mark changes of trust, not protocols.

choices.text: HTTPS flows are left out of the diagram
choices.why: Most of the portal's flows are HTTPS and all are drawn.

choices.text: It names the transport, not the data
choices.why: Right. The label says what moves: an exam PDF, a booking.

prompt: Somebody draws an arrow straight from the records database to a backup store. What does the DFD rule say?

choices.text: Draw the backup job between them
choices.why: Right. Data does not move by itself; the code that copies it is where things go wrong.

choices.text: It is fine, since backups are internal
choices.why: Internal or not, a flow needs a process at one end.

choices.text: Remove the backup, which is infrastructure and has no data
choices.why: A backup holds every record; it is very much data.

choices.text: Turn both stores into one
choices.why: They are two copies in two places, with two sets of readers.

prompt: "The worker runs at 20:00 and then sends the reminders." Where does that sentence belong?

choices.text: On the flow from worker to SMS provider, as its label
choices.why: The label names data, not timing.

choices.text: Inside the worker's circle
choices.why: The circle names the process; it does not hold its schedule.

choices.text: In a sequence diagram beside the DFD
choices.why: Right. A DFD has no order and no conditions.

choices.text: Nowhere, since timing never matters to threats
choices.why: Sometimes it does, and then a sequence diagram says it.

prompt: What does a trust boundary mark?

choices.text: Where the firewall is
choices.why: The firewall is one boundary of many.

choices.text: Where one server ends and another starts
choices.why: That is an infrastructure diagram.

choices.text: Where the level of trust changes
choices.why: Right. Anything crossing it has to be checked on arrival.

choices.text: Where a control is enforced
choices.why: Drawing a boundary does not say anything enforces it.

prompt: Which of these call for a boundary between two parts of the portal? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: one answers the internet, the other only the private network
choices.why: Network reachability differs.

choices.text: one runs Vereda's code, the other a vendor's
choices.why: Who controls the code differs.

choices.text: one is written in Python, the other in Go
choices.why: The language does not change trust.

choices.text: one is used by patients, the other by staff who read every record
choices.why: The people and their privileges differ.

prompt: The console sits behind a line labelled clinic network, and it answers from the internet. What does the lesson call that line?

choices.text: A finding
choices.why: Right. A boundary with nothing enforcing it is a finding in itself.

choices.text: A mistake in the drawing that should be erased
choices.why: The line shows the intent; erasing it hides the gap.

choices.text: A control that protects the console
choices.why: A drawn line protects nothing.

choices.text: A detail for level 2 diagrams
choices.why: It is a level 1 fact about exposure.

prompt: Order the three questions a crossing raises, as the section lists them.
items: Who sent this, and how do we know?
Can it be read or changed on the way?
Can it be sent too much, or too large?

prompt: Why is the flow from the portal into the private network worth examining?

choices.text: It is the only flow that uses PostgreSQL
choices.why: Two others reach the database too.

choices.text: It crosses the internet
choices.why: It stays inside Vereda's cloud.

choices.text: Patients send it directly
choices.why: The portal sends it, on their behalf.

choices.text: If the portal is taken over, its checks are what protect every record
choices.why: Right. The single box round the cloud hides this flow.

prompt: What does a level 0, or context, diagram show?

choices.text: Every function of every process, at full detail
choices.why: That would be unreadable.

choices.text: The system as one process and everything it talks to
choices.why: Right. Nothing inside is shown.

choices.text: The servers, the network and how they connect
choices.why: That is infrastructure.

choices.text: Only the trust boundaries
choices.why: Boundaries need the elements they separate.

prompt: Which part of the portal does the lesson say might deserve a level 2 diagram?

choices.text: The upload, which takes files from anybody
choices.why: Right: complex and exposed, it takes files from anybody.

choices.text: The reminder worker, which reads a table and calls one API
choices.why: Simple and not exposed: not worth it.

choices.text: Every process, for completeness
choices.why: That is how a model outgrows its design.

choices.text: The SMS provider
choices.why: An external entity is not opened: it is not yours.

prompt: Checking that every flow entering a process at one level enters one of its parts at the next is called ___ the diagram.
Level 0 shows a flow of 'insurance number' from the patient. Level 1 has no flow with that label. What follows?

choices.text: Level 1 is more detailed, so it wins
choices.why: Detail does not make it right.

choices.text: One of the two levels is wrong
choices.why: Right: a missing flow below or an invented one above, and both are worth knowing.

choices.text: Nothing; levels are drawn independently
choices.why: Levels must not contradict each other.

choices.text: The flow belongs in a sequence diagram
choices.why: It is data, so it belongs in the DFD.

prompt: This is the portal's level 1 diagram without its words. Put each name where it belongs.
hint: Count the arrows: three processes write to one store.

prompt: How many of the portal's twelve flows cross a trust boundary?
Three processes reach the records database. Why does the lesson care?

choices.text: Three writers make the database slow
choices.why: Performance is not the question here.

choices.text: A data store may only have one writer
choices.why: There is no such rule.

choices.text: If they share one account, the weakest decides what an attacker gets
choices.why: Right, and one of them uses the owner's password.

choices.text: It means the database should be outside the private network
choices.why: That would make it worse.

prompt: Which flow is the only one from a vendor into Vereda?

choices.text: The reminder sent to the SMS provider
choices.why: That goes out of Vereda, not in.

choices.text: The charge for a session
choices.why: The portal sends that to the gateway.

choices.text: The upload of an exam PDF
choices.why: A patient sends that, not a vendor.

choices.text: The payment webhook, flow 7
choices.why: Right, flow 7: payment state arrives this way and nowhere else.

prompt: The design says the console is for the clinics, and it answers from the internet. What do both honest drawings have in common?

choices.text: Both remove the clinic network boundary
choices.why: The boundary stays; the gap is written down.

choices.text: Both record the gap instead of drawing only the intent
choices.why: Right: a flow marked as a finding, or an assumption to check.

choices.text: Both move the console into the private network
choices.why: Drawing it there would not make it true.

choices.text: Both wait until a penetration test confirms it
choices.why: The builders already know; it is written now.

prompt: Which of these drawings break a rule of the notation? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: an arrow from the records database to the backup store
choices.why: No process at either end.

choices.text: an arrow from the patient to the payment gateway
choices.why: Two external entities: outside the model.

choices.text: two arrows between the patient and the portal, one each way
choices.why: That is the right way to draw a request and a response.

choices.text: an arrow from the portal to the exam files with no label
choices.why: Every flow names its data.

prompt: What is lost when the portal, the console and the worker are drawn as one box called the backend?

choices.text: Nothing, because they share a database
choices.why: Sharing a store is itself something to see.

choices.text: Only the names of the three programs
choices.why: Different users, privileges and exposure disappear.

choices.text: The flows to the SMS provider
choices.why: Those can still be drawn to the box.

choices.text: The boundary between what patients reach and what staff reach
choices.why: Right, and with it the question of a patient reaching staff functions.

prompt: ana says the worker calls the portal's API instead of reading the database. If that is right, what changes in the drawing?

choices.text: Flow 11 goes to the portal
choices.why: Right, and the worker never needed the database password.

choices.text: Nothing, since the data is the same
choices.why: Where it comes from is what the DFD shows.

choices.text: The worker moves out of the private network
choices.why: Where it runs is a separate fact.

choices.text: Flow 12 disappears
choices.why: Reminders still go to the SMS provider.

prompt: In pytm, what is the difference between an Actor and an ExternalEntity?

choices.text: An Actor sits inside the system and an ExternalEntity outside
choices.why: Both are outside your control.

choices.text: An ExternalEntity cannot be in a boundary
choices.why: Both are placed with inBoundary.

choices.text: An Actor is a person; an ExternalEntity is another system
choices.why: Right: the patient and the SMS provider.

choices.text: There is none; they are two names for one class
choices.why: They are separate classes.

prompt: Why is the portal a Server in model.py while the reminder worker is a Process?

choices.text: The portal is the bigger and more important program
choices.why: Size is not the distinction.

choices.text: Only a Server can write to a database in pytm
choices.why: The worker reads the database too.

choices.text: The portal answers requests and keeps sessions
choices.why: Right, which lets pytm ask about sessions.

choices.text: A Process cannot be in a boundary
choices.why: The worker is in the private network.

prompt: flows.py marks flow 4, portal to exam files, as crossing. Both ends are in Vereda's cloud. Why?

choices.text: Their store sits in the private network, a zone of its own
choices.why: Right: nested boundaries count as two zones.

choices.text: Every flow that reaches a data store counts as a crossing
choices.why: Flow 11 reaches a store and does not cross.

choices.text: Uploads always cross boundaries
choices.why: Crossing is about boundaries, not the kind of data.

choices.text: pytm counts every HTTPS flow as a crossing of some kind
choices.why: The program compares boundaries only.

prompt: Why does .gitignore list model.json?

choices.text: It holds secrets
choices.why: It holds the model, nothing secret.

choices.text: git cannot store JSON
choices.why: It can.

choices.text: pytm refuses to run if it is committed
choices.why: pytm does not look at git.

choices.text: It is produced from model.py
choices.why: Right: commit the source, not what is generated from it.

prompt: Vereda adds a partner lab that uploads exam results straight into the exam files bucket. What should the drawing gain?

choices.text: Nothing: uploads are already flow 3
choices.why: Flow 3 comes from patients, through the portal.

choices.text: A new outsider, a boundary, and its flow
choices.why: Right, and that flow arrives in the private network with no process of Vereda's in front of it.

choices.text: A second portal
choices.why: No new process was described.

choices.text: A note on the exam files store
choices.why: A new outsider and a new way in are drawn, not noted.

prompt: Strictly, which rule does the partner lab's direct upload break?

choices.text: A flow needs a process at one end at least
choices.why: Right: lab to bucket has none, so some code is missing from the drawing, or from the design.

choices.text: Every flow needs a label
choices.why: It can be labelled exam result.

choices.text: No flow may cross two boundaries
choices.why: There is no such rule.

choices.text: External entities may not touch data stores
choices.why: That is the same rule said loosely; the one in the lesson is about processes.

prompt: Match each part of the portal to the pytm class model.py gives it.
